newsitem.title: UK: UK gilts this week - market may be over the worst.
newsitem.headline: UK gilts this week - market may be over the worst.

text.p: After taking a severe knock last week on stronger than expected jobs and inflation data, UK gilts should enjoy a steadier week with the market coming round to the view that the worst news is probably out of the way.

Gilts got off to a good start after October PSBR data on Monday showed a much larger than expected 4.4 billion stg debt repayment. Wednesday's retail sales numbers were also expected to be supportive, analysts said.
"Going forward, the worst news is probably out of the way for gilts, which should permit a slow grind higher," said Don Smith and Philip Tyson of HSBC Markets in their weekly comment.
Next week's budget on November 26 will also loom large in the market's mind.
HSBC expects net tax cuts of two to three billion stg, which it regards as the limit of what the market would consider acceptable, and says a tight budget would be well received.
"Against this backdrop, sterling is set to retain its buoyancy in the coming weeks and gilts look cheap both on an absolute and a relative basis," Smith and Tyson wrote.
They see the 10-year gilt-Bund spread narrowing back to 175 basis points from around 184 on Monday and a high of over 200 last week.

Tom Rayner, analyst at Societe Generale, agreed a 175 basis point spread is probably the best that can be hoped for this week. "If anything the spread will do well to stay around 180 as the budget approaches," he said. "I'm not very confident that it could tighten much further at this stage and it could even push back out again through 190." Rayner sees the spread in a range of 10 points on either side of 180, possibly narrowing towards 175, if retail sales are softer than expected.
Economists forecast a 0.5 percent jump in October sales, taking the year-on-year rate up to 4.1 percent. In September, retail sales dropped by 0.3 percent.
Rayner noted that strong demand emerged when the spread widened to around 200 and says this should remain a strong cap.
"We're trading 10 or 11 basis points above Italy and I think gilts have to look fairly good value there," he said.
Expectations for UK interest rates have swung significantly in the direction of further tightening since the unexpected quarter-point rise in base rates to 6.0 percent on October 30.

After a spectacular 40,000 fall in unemployment last week and the surge in inflation, the short sterling strip is pricing in a 75-basis point increase in rates to around 6.75 percent by the end of the first quarter.

"The fact that it has already priced in fairly aggressive moves might mean that we've seen the worst for a while on the short-term rates," Rayner said. "Any further curve-flattening would have to come from more good performance at the longer end and I don't think we are going to see that."
Continued strength in sterling, which hit a fresh four-year high against the dollar in Europe on Monday, should remain supportive for gilts.
Michael Derks and James Mitchell of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said the performance of sterling had more than offset the dismal performance of gilts over the last month.
"Given our belief that almost all of the bad news is now priced in, the front end is beginning to represent good value," they wrote in their Market Strategy Monthly.
They hope underlying inflation will improve in November from the shock jump to 3.3 percent in October as positive base effects show up and the strong pound brings down petrol prices.
"We recommend that domestic investors unwind Bund exposure hedged into sterling in favour of gilts at a spread of 200 bp."

Gerard Lyons of DKB International expects the Bank of England to continue to push aggressively for further interest rate increases and he anticipates a move in February, but not as sharply as the short sterling strip does.
"Gilt yields look attractive as the market has discounted too much bad news," he said.
